1.why: Verify succeeds only when the submitted code/token matches the reset secrets stored on that same session, which is bound to the accountId set at recovery-request.

2.why: Reset secrets live only on the requester’s session map entry; another user’s session has different manualCode/resetToken values, so the same code does not authenticate them.

3.why: password-change updates only the account hash and current session stage; no code invalidates other existing sessions for that account.

4.why: Bun.serve is configured with TLS cert/key and HTTP is rejected via x-forwarded-proto, but the TLS protocol version is not explicitly pinned in code.

5.why: Passwords are bcrypt-hashed, but reset tokens, manual codes, and session user fields are stored in memory as plaintext, not encrypted.

6.why: There is no real email path; the API returns manualRecoveryCode and verificationUrl in JSON and the client prints them to the visible Logs panel.

7.why: Inputs are format-validated (validId/validCode/validPass) and the UI assigns only textContent; there is validation more than classical sanitization libraries.

8.why: verificationPath/Url are fixed to the local /verify route on localhost; no user-controlled redirect target is honored.

9.why: No email HTML templates exist; dynamic UI strings use textContent only and never interpolate user input as HTML/scripts.

10.why: Recovery codes, verification URLs, and MFA codes are deliberately written to console and the on-page Logs list.

11.why: Password hashes use bcrypt, but MFA_CODE is the hardcoded secret "246810" and the initial bcrypt hash is embedded in source.

12.why: MFA is always the fixed default 246810, and a known demo password hash seeds accounts, so default-style credentials are present.

13.why: allowed/fail implement progressive per-action/identifier/IP throttling that returns 429 after repeated failures.

14.why: Unknown identifiers are bound to sinkId and receive the same recovery response shape, avoiding existence oracles.

15.why: manualCode and resetToken are produced with crypto.getRandomValues (base64url), short-lived, single-use, and stored only on that user’s session.
